title: Enhanced recovery and postoperative pain
blurb: Explain an enhanced recovery programme and choose, give and review multimodal analgesia the way NICE NG180 sets out.
question: Mr Okoro, 70, is on day 1 of an enhanced recovery programme after an open bowel resection. He is eating and drinking, takes regular oral paracetamol and ibuprofen, but his pain is 7/10 when he coughs and he will not walk. An oral immediate-release opioid is prescribed as required. What should the nurse do?

teach.h: What an enhanced recovery programme is
teach.body: An enhanced recovery programme is a planned bundle of care that runs through the whole surgical journey: before, during and after the operation. NICE NG180 says offer one to people having elective major or complex surgery, and that it must include preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative components. Plain English: get the person as fit as possible before surgery, keep the operation as gentle on the body as possible, then get them eating, drinking, pain-controlled and moving early so they recover faster and safely.

steps.label: Before surgery
steps.sub: Stop smoking, cut alcohol, treat iron-deficiency anaemia

steps.label: Fasting kept short
steps.sub: Clear fluids to 2 h; carbohydrate drinks considered

steps.label: During surgery
steps.sub: Intraoperative care planned as part of the bundle

steps.label: After surgery
steps.sub: Multimodal analgesia, early eating and drinking

steps.label: Moving and home
steps.sub: Pain controlled so they cough, walk and go home

teach.caption: NG180 1.3.2–1.3.4 (prehabilitation), 1.4.2 (carbohydrate drinks before major abdominal surgery); clear fluids to 2 hours from the 2026 fasting consensus.
Examples from the NG180 'Terms used'. The programme is for ELECTIVE major or complex surgery.

teach.body: NICE says offer a multimodal approach: analgesics from different classes combined to manage postoperative pain. Plan it with the person BEFORE surgery, taking into account comorbidities, age, frailty, kidney and liver function, allergies, current medicines and cognition, and include their pain history, preferences and discharge plans. Immediate postoperative pain means pain in the first 24 hours after surgery. Consider pre-emptive analgesia for when local anaesthesia wears off.

teach.text: Intravenous does not mean better. NICE says do NOT give IV paracetamol or an IV NSAID when the person can take oral medicine. And oral ibuprofen is offered for all severities of pain EXCEPT after hip fracture surgery, which follows the hip fracture guideline instead.

teach.body: Mr Okoro, 70, had an open right hemicolectomy and is on a surgical ward. He is drinking and eating soup, taking oral paracetamol and ibuprofen, but scores his pain 7/10 on coughing and refuses to walk. His as-required oral immediate-release opioid has not been given 'because he hasn't asked'. The nurse offers and gives it now, explains why moving matters, and reassesses pain on coughing and walking. NICE: give the oral opioid as soon as the person can eat and drink, and adjust the dose to help functional recovery.

items: Assess pain at rest AND on movement: can they cough, sit out and walk?
Give regular paracetamol and ibuprofen (unless contraindicated) and offer the opioid when pain is moderate to severe.
Prompt a switch from IV to oral analgesia once the person can take oral medicine.
Encourage drinking and eating as soon as clinically possible, and early mobilisation.
Reassess after each dose and escalate if pain stops the person recovering.
Offer enhanced recovery for elective major or complex surgery; it covers pre, intra and postoperative care.
Multimodal analgesia, planned with the person before surgery.
Oral paracetamol before and after surgery whatever the pain; IV only if oral impossible.
Oral ibuprofen for all severities, except after hip fracture surgery.
Oral immediate-release opioid for expected moderate to severe pain, dosed for coughing and mobilising; PCA or epidural if oral is not possible.

summary: You can now explain who should be offered an enhanced recovery programme and what it contains. You can also choose and review postoperative analgesia in line with NICE NG180, aiming for pain control that lets the person cough, eat and move.

A.q: Four people are booked on a surgical ward's lists this week. Under NICE NG180, which person should be offered an enhanced recovery programme?
options: Ms Ray, having an emergency laparotomy for a perforation
Mr Dunn, booked for an elective knee arthroscopy
Mr Hale, booked for an elective total knee replacement
Mrs Cole, booked for an elective primary inguinal hernia repair
A.why: NG180 rec 1.2.1 offers enhanced recovery to people having ELECTIVE major or complex surgery. Total joint replacement is listed as major or complex surgery.

whyNot.0: A laparotomy is major, but this one is an emergency; rec 1.2.1 covers elective major or complex surgery.
whyNot.1: Knee arthroscopy is an NG180 example of intermediate surgery, not major or complex surgery.
whyNot.3: Primary inguinal hernia repair is an NG180 example of intermediate surgery.

A.q: A patient asks why she is being offered regular oral paracetamol both before and after her operation. What does NICE NG180 recommend?
options: Before and after surgery, whatever the pain severity
After surgery once pain reaches a moderate score
Intravenously for the first 24 hours after surgery
Before surgery, then as required whenever she asks for it
A.why: NG180 rec 1.6.5: offer oral paracetamol before and after surgery irrespective of pain severity. It is a foundation of multimodal analgesia.

whyNot.1: Paracetamol is not held back for moderate pain; NICE offers it whatever the severity.
whyNot.2: Rec 1.6.6: do not offer IV paracetamol unless the person cannot take oral medicine.
whyNot.3: NICE recommends it after surgery as well, not only on request; waiting for her to ask defeats the multimodal plan.

A.q: In NICE NG180, what does the term 'immediate postoperative pain' describe?
options: Pain until the person first eats after surgery
Pain during the first 48 hours after surgery
Pain during the first 72 hours after surgery
Pain during the first 24 hours after surgery
A.why: NG180 defines immediate postoperative pain as pain during the first 24 hours after surgery.

whyNot.0: The definition is time-based, not linked to the first meal.
whyNot.1: 48 hours is the NG125 wound-cleansing time point, not this definition.
whyNot.2: 72 hours is not the NG180 definition; it is 24 hours.

B.q: Ms Ward, 52, is back on the ward after an elective open hysterectomy. She is drinking and eating toast, and her pain is expected to be moderate to severe for the next day. Which opioid plan matches NICE NG180?
options: Modified-release oral opioid twice daily for a week
Oral immediate-release opioid, dosed so she can cough and walk
Intramuscular morphine every 4 hours, given whenever she requests it
PCA as the first choice after all major open surgery
B.why: NG180 rec 1.6.10: offer an oral immediate-release opioid if pain is expected to be moderate to severe, give it as soon as the person can eat and drink, and adjust the dose to help functional recovery such as coughing and mobilising.

whyNot.0: NICE recommends an immediate-release opioid for immediate postoperative pain, not a fixed modified-release course.
whyNot.2: She can eat and drink, so NICE recommends the oral route; intramuscular injections are not part of the NG180 plan.
whyNot.3: PCA (or an epidural) is offered to people who CANNOT take oral opioids; Ms Ward can.

B.q: Mr Benn, 45, is vomiting and cannot take oral medicine on the evening of his laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The team plans an intravenous NSAID for his immediate postoperative pain. Which choice follows NICE NG180?
options: A COX-2 inhibitor in preference to a traditional NSAID
IV ketamine infusion in place of an NSAID
A traditional NSAID in preference to a COX-2 inhibitor
IV NSAID withheld until 24 hours after surgery
B.why: NG180 rec 1.6.9: if offering an IV NSAID for immediate postoperative pain (allowed when oral medicine cannot be taken, 1.6.8), choose a traditional NSAID rather than a COX-2 inhibitor.

whyNot.0: This reverses the recommendation: NICE prefers a traditional NSAID over a COX-2 inhibitor.
whyNot.1: NICE suggests considering a single dose of IV ketamine in specific situations, not an infusion replacing an NSAID.
whyNot.3: There is no 24-hour wait; an IV NSAID can be used now because he cannot take oral medicine.

B.q: Mrs Ali, 81, cannot take oral opioids after major open abdominal surgery. The team offers her a choice of PCA or a continuous epidural. Which factor in her history makes NICE highlight the benefits of an epidural?
options: She has cognitive impairment
Her surgery was laparoscopic
She expects mild pain
She wants to self-administer
B.why: NG180 rec 1.6.11 asks teams to take into account the benefits of a continuous epidural for people having major or complex open-torso surgery, those expected to have severe pain, or those with cognitive impairment.

whyNot.1: The epidural benefit is highlighted for open-torso surgery, not laparoscopic surgery.
whyNot.2: Epidural benefits are highlighted when SEVERE pain is expected, not mild pain.
whyNot.3: Wanting to control her own doses fits PCA (patient-controlled analgesia), not the epidural factors.

C.q: Mr Okoro, 70, is on day 1 after an open right hemicolectomy in an enhanced recovery programme. He is eating and drinking and takes regular oral paracetamol and ibuprofen. His pain is 7/10 on coughing and he will not walk to the chair. His as-required oral immediate-release opioid has not been given since surgery. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Wait for the physiotherapist to judge his mobility first
Request IV paracetamol in addition to his oral dose
Ask for his PCA to be restarted until he can walk
Give the oral opioid now and reassess pain on coughing
C.why: His pain is moderate to severe and he can eat and drink, so NG180 rec 1.6.10 supports giving the oral immediate-release opioid now and adjusting it so he can cough and mobilise. Reassessing on movement shows whether it worked.

whyNot.0: Delaying analgesia leaves him unable to cough or move; pain control comes first so that physiotherapy can succeed.
whyNot.1: He is already taking oral paracetamol; IV paracetamol is not offered when oral medicine can be taken, and doubling paracetamol risks overdose.
whyNot.2: PCA is for people who cannot take oral opioids; he can, and has an oral opioid prescribed.

C.q: Mrs Hughes, 66, has iron-deficiency anaemia and is booked for an elective colectomy in 6 weeks as part of an enhanced recovery programme. Daily oral iron is making her nauseated and constipated, and she is thinking of stopping it. What does NICE NG180 suggest?
options: Stop the iron, as surgery itself corrects the anaemia
Consider an alternate-day oral iron regimen instead
Book a blood transfusion for the morning of surgery
Double each dose so the course finishes sooner
C.why: NG180 rec 1.3.4 says treat iron-deficiency anaemia before surgery, and rec 1.3.5 suggests considering an alternate-day oral iron regimen for people who have side effects.

whyNot.0: Treating anaemia before surgery is part of preparation (1.3.4); surgery does not correct iron deficiency.
whyNot.2: A planned transfusion on the day is not the NG180 approach to known iron deficiency weeks before surgery.
whyNot.3: A higher dose would be likely to worsen her side effects; NICE suggests alternate days instead.

C.q: At pre-assessment Mr Doyle, 74, who has CKD and mild cognitive impairment, is booked for an elective hip replacement. The nurse begins planning his postoperative pain relief. What does NICE NG180 say this discussion should take into account?
options: His kidney function, cognition and pain history
The standard ward protocol used for every hip replacement
His anaesthetist's preference, decided on the day
The strongest opioid available, to avoid any pain
C.why: NG180 rec 1.6.1: discuss pain management before surgery, taking into account comorbidities, age, frailty, kidney and liver function, allergies, current medicines and cognitive function, plus the person's pain history and preferences.

whyNot.1: NICE asks for an individual plan based on his clinical features, not one protocol for everyone.
whyNot.2: The discussion happens with him before surgery, not as a decision made on the day without him.
whyNot.3: NICE recommends multimodal analgesia matched to the person, with opioids for expected moderate to severe pain, not the strongest drug by default.

reteach.title: Pain control is a tool for moving
reteach.question: Why does an enhanced recovery programme care so much about pain scores when the person coughs or walks, not just at rest?

blocks.body: The point of postoperative analgesia in enhanced recovery is function: being able to breathe deeply, cough, eat, sit out and walk soon after surgery. NICE asks for the opioid dose to be adjusted to help functional recovery, such as coughing and mobilising. So a patient who is comfortable lying still but cannot cough has not got adequate pain control.

steps.sub: If oral opioids are not possible

blocks.text: Switch IV to oral as soon as the person can take oral medicine: NICE does not offer IV paracetamol or IV NSAIDs to people who can swallow.

explain.body: Offer enhanced recovery to people having elective major or complex surgery, such as colonic resection, total abdominal hysterectomy or total joint replacement. It has three parts: preoperative (prehabilitation such as stopping smoking, reducing alcohol, treating anaemia), intraoperative and postoperative.

test.q: Which description of an enhanced recovery programme matches NICE NG180?
options: A postoperative mobility plan run by physiotherapists
A discharge checklist completed on the day of going home
A bundle covering pre, intra and postoperative care
A preoperative clinic focused on fitness for anaesthesia
test.why: NG180 rec 1.2.2: use an enhanced recovery programme that includes preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative components.

whyNot.0: Mobilisation is one postoperative part, but the programme spans the whole journey.
whyNot.1: Discharge planning is included, but the programme starts well before surgery.
whyNot.3: Preoperative preparation is one component; the programme also covers surgery and recovery.

explain.body: Oral paracetamol before and after surgery whatever the pain; IV paracetamol only if oral is not possible. Oral ibuprofen for immediate postoperative pain of all severities, except after hip fracture surgery. An IV NSAID is not offered unless oral is impossible, and then a traditional NSAID is chosen over a COX-2 inhibitor.

test.q: Mrs Grey, 68, is eating breakfast on day 1 after a knee replacement. Her chart still shows IV paracetamol 6-hourly. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask the prescriber to review a switch to oral paracetamol
Continue the IV paracetamol for the full first 72 hours after surgery
Add oral paracetamol alongside the IV doses
Stop all paracetamol now that she is eating
test.why: NG180 rec 1.6.6: do not offer IV paracetamol unless the person cannot take oral medicine. She can, so the route should be reviewed and switched.

whyNot.1: There is no 72-hour IV period; the IV route is for people who cannot take oral medicine.
whyNot.2: Giving oral and IV paracetamol together risks exceeding the maximum dose.
whyNot.3: NICE offers paracetamol after surgery whatever the pain level, so it should continue orally.

explain.body: Offer an oral immediate-release opioid if pain is expected to be moderate to severe, as soon as the person can eat and drink, dosed for functional recovery. If oral opioids cannot be taken, offer a choice of PCA or a continuous epidural; the epidural's benefits matter most for major open-torso surgery, expected severe pain or cognitive impairment.

root.label: Can the person take oral opioids?

test.q: Which person after surgery should be offered a choice of PCA or a continuous epidural under NICE NG180?
options: One with mild pain who is eating and drinking
One who cannot take oral opioids after a laparotomy
One with moderate pain who would prefer to take tablets by mouth
One who is due home on the day of surgery
test.why: NG180 rec 1.6.11: for people who cannot take oral opioids, offer a choice of PCA or a continuous epidural.

whyNot.0: Mild pain in someone eating and drinking is managed with oral paracetamol and ibuprofen.
whyNot.2: Someone who can take tablets and has moderate pain is offered an oral immediate-release opioid.
whyNot.3: Day-case patients going home need oral analgesia they can continue at home.

explain.body: Enhanced recovery aims to restore normal function quickly. The 2026 fasting consensus advises resuming fluids and diet as soon as clinically feasible after anaesthesia, and NICE NG89 encourages mobilisation as soon as possible. Analgesia is judged by what it lets the person do: cough, sit out and walk.
explain.cite: Anaesthesia 2026 fasting consensus; NICE NG89 rec 1.3.14; NG180 rec 1.6.10

test.q: According to NICE NG180, what should guide the dose of an oral opioid after surgery?
options: A pain score of zero while lying in bed
Sleeping right through the first night after the operation
Discharge within 24 hours of the operation
Recovery of function such as coughing and walking
test.why: NG180 rec 1.6.10: adjust the opioid dose to help the person achieve functional recovery, such as coughing and mobilising, as soon as possible.

whyNot.0: Comfort at rest is not the target; pain on movement is what limits recovery.
whyNot.1: Sleep matters, but NICE links the dose to functional recovery.
whyNot.2: Length of stay is an outcome of the programme, not the measure NICE uses to adjust the dose.
